source.title: ILDR: Geometric Early Detection of Grokking

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains small transformers on algorithmic tasks and tests grokking timing with a new representation-geometry measure, rather than reproducing the original method.
record.gate_note: Rows cover reported grokking-transition timings and ILDR lead times, training-fraction results, and weight-decay interventions. The text describes training accuracy reaching near-perfect levels before generalization, but the results do not report per-run training-accuracy timing. Weight norm and Grokfast are included only where compared as grokking-detection signals; their values are not evidence about artifact explanations.
record.test_reason: The study reports held-out generalization on small algorithmic tasks, tests whether a geometric progress measure anticipates it, and intervenes on weight decay. These results bear on V1, the progress-measure component of V2, and the weight-decay component of V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that ILDR usually anticipates the held-out threshold on these algorithmic tasks and that flag-triggered optimizer interventions change transition timing. They interpret this as mechanistically suggestive, not direct circuit identification. Their claimed 18.6% training reduction counts flag-to-grok intervals rather than actual ILDR+200 stopping savings, and most stopped runs have poor accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: Uses small transformers and algorithmic training tasks with held-out grokking measurements, but proposes ILDR as a new detector and includes additional tasks, sweeps, and interventions rather than simply reproducing the original study.
record.method_sensitivity: The ILDR lead varies with task, modulus, model depth, and training fraction; the reported training-fraction and several sensitivity sweeps use a single seed. The study also reports seed-dependent early-stopping validation accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Post-grok ILDR CV falls from 121.8% to 61.6%, with a reported variance ratio of 1696.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representation-geometry signal variability changes after generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: ILDR+200 stopping gives validation accuracy of 7.1%–99.3%; reported savings omit the grace period.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: An early geometric flag does not guarantee successful early stopping.

record.problems: Many sensitivity sweeps use a single seed; detection thresholds were selected by a preliminary sweep on one held-out seed. Training-accuracy saturation and detailed held-out accuracy trajectories are not reported in the results. Early-stopping validation accuracy varies widely, including 7.1% for one seed. The authors report 41% overhead when evaluating every 100 steps.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported grokking-transition or ILDR outcome was left out.

untested.parts: Per-run training-accuracy saturation, the subsequent delay measured from that saturation, and chance-to-near-perfect jump trajectories are not reported.
Identifiable generalizing circuits, their gradual formation, later removal of memorizing components, and causal attribution to those mechanisms are not measured.
Non-algorithmic data, initialization-scale or weight-norm switching, and lazy-to-rich transitions.
Relative circuit efficiency or norm, a critical dataset size, and ungrokking below that size.
Identification and comparison of learned algorithms across runs, architectures, or hyperparameters.
Optimizer-instability and floating-point/softmax explanations, including controls that remove such artifacts.

missing.what: The oscillation run also reports grokking at 5100 and ILDR at 3800, a positive 1300-step lead; r24 records only variability.
Baseline intervention runs reach >95% at 6400, 4800, and 5500, with corresponding ILDR intervention triggers at 5100, 4300, and 4600. Record these paired precursor timings separately.

record.verdict_notes: Use only the supplied text. Missing measurements are untested parts, not evidence of partial or absent effects. Detector lead times do not by themselves establish V1's full delayed-generalization trajectory. All timings are quantized to 100 steps; the high-fraction detector comparison is constrained by its step-3000 baseline. Neither repeated timing values nor consistent geometry identifies a shared learned algorithm.

versions.untested_parts: The results do not report when training accuracy saturates or give detailed test-accuracy trajectories showing a chance-to-near-perfect jump. The dependence on training-set size is assessed in a single-seed sweep.

ILDR is a geometric progress measure, but the study does not identify a Fourier or other specific algorithmic circuit, track memorizing components being removed, or establish that circuit formation causes the transition.
The experiments use algorithmic tasks; they do not test non-algorithmic data or initialization-scale/lazy-to-rich changes.
No LLM pretraining or realistic-data fine-tuning is tested.

Weight-decay changes are tested for their effect on grokking timing, but the study does not demonstrate that they select a more efficient generalizing circuit or test a critical dataset size or ungrokking below it.
The study does not identify and compare algorithms learned across runs.
The study does not test adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point/softmax artifacts as explanations for grokking.
